analysis.one_liner: Requires cost-benefit analysis, congressional review, and new court challenges for major federal regulations.
analysis.headline: Introduced by one member with zero cosponsors, the bill never got a hearing, markup, or vote in any House committee before the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced federal agencies to prove, through a formal cost-benefit analysis, that every 'major rule' — one costing the economy $50 million or more — benefits society more than it costs, and to pick the cheapest alternative. Major rules could not take effect for at least 45 days after being sent to Congress, and either chamber could kill a rule with a resolution, using fast-track procedures. It would also have suspended all statutory deadlines for issuing rules and stripped courts of their power to enforce them, let any regulated party sue to overturn agency interpretations, and barred rules that extend federal authority beyond what a statute strictly requires.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses regulated by expensive federal rules — manufacturers, energy and chemical companies, and other firms subject to environmental, health, and safety regulation — would gain new tools to delay, challenge, and overturn rules: mandatory cost-benefit analyses, court review of agency designations, petitions to reopen old rules, and a congressional veto over major rules. Small businesses would gain an explicit right to sue over agencies' small-business impact analyses.

how_it_helps.text: Requires agencies to show that a major rule's benefits outweigh its costs and beat every reasonable alternative, including market-based mechanisms, before it can be issued [S2][S3].
Lets any person subject to a major rule — including rules already in effect — petition to force a new cost-benefit review that can lead to the rule being revoked or weakened [S3].
Gives affected small businesses the right to go to court when an agency claims a rule won't significantly affect small entities, and lets courts order the analysis redone or freeze the rule [S3].
Bars agencies from issuing rules that expand federal authority beyond what existing statutes require [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: People who rely on federal health, safety, and environmental protections would bear the cost: rules protecting air, water, workplaces, and consumer products would take months longer, face lawsuits at every stage, and could be vetoed by a single chamber's resolution. Agencies would carry heavy new analysis and reporting burdens, and statutory deadlines Congress set — for example, deadlines to act on known hazards — could go unenforced because courts would lose jurisdiction to enforce them.

drawbacks.text: Cost-benefit analysis works well for costs that show up on a ledger but poorly for benefits like avoided deaths and illnesses, so requiring benefits to outweigh quantifiable costs tends to screen out protective rules [S3].
The bill suspends all statutory rulemaking deadlines and suspends courts' power to enforce them, so rules that Congress ordered agencies to write could stall indefinitely [S3].
A single chamber could kill a major rule through expedited procedures with limited debate, letting a congressional minority of the moment block protections a law already authorized [S3].
Allowing petitions to reopen and re-litigate existing major rules, including rules already in force, would inject uncertainty into longstanding protections [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real case for the transparency pieces — publishing draft cost-benefit analyses and risk assessments would let the public see what agencies are weighing. But the bill's core design points the other way: hard litigation triggers, suspended deadlines, a one-chamber veto over rules, and a mandate to choose the cheapest compliant alternative all make it structurally harder for agencies to issue and keep protective rules. The savings would flow mainly to regulated firms; the risk of weaker, slower protections would fall on the public.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees and then to subcommittees, and it sat there without a hearing, markup, or vote until the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. David McIntosh introduced the bill on February 3, 1995, and it was referred to the Government Reform and Oversight, Judiciary, and Rules Committees [S1][S5].
No member of the House from either party signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
In February and March 1995 the bill was referred to subcommittees of the Government Reform and Oversight and Judiciary Committees; the record shows no further action after that [S5].
The bill never received a committee vote or floor vote and died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal agencies kept their existing authority to issue and defend health, safety, and environmental rules without the new cost-benefit, deadline-suspension, and congressional-disapproval hurdles. Regulated industries did not get the new tools to challenge and overturn major rules. McIntosh and the 1995 regulatory-reform movement lost this vehicle, though similar provisions advanced in other bills that Congress.

for.name: Rep. David McIntosh
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to three committees; he was a leading figure in the 104th Congress's regulatory-reform effort

against.name: House Government Reform and Oversight, Judiciary, and Rules Committees
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill; after subcommittee referral in February and March 1995, the record shows no markup, hearing vote, or further action

against.name: Members of the House
against.what_they_did: None signed on as a cosponsor, from either party

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Republican, but with zero cosponsors and no votes, the record shows no partisan lineup on this bill at all.

industries.industry: Regulated manufacturers, energy, and chemical firms
industries.note: The bill would have made every major rule easier to delay, sue over, and kill through mandatory cost-benefit analysis, judicial review, petitions to reopen existing rules, and a congressional disapproval mechanism. The savings would come from compliance costs; the offsetting cost would be weaker or slower health, safety, and environmental protections for the public.

Small entities would gain an explicit one-year window to sue over agencies' small-business impact certifications, and courts could freeze rules that skip the analysis. That eases compliance burdens, though it is the narrowest piece of the bill.

Agencies would face mandatory cost-benefit and risk assessments, peer review, presidential oversight, congressional reporting, and loss of court-backed deadlines. Their core mission — writing and defending protective rules — would become slower and more litigation-prone, which is where the public's stake in strong rules sits.
